newsitem.title: USA: Philadelphia mayor proposes new tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Philadelphia mayor proposes new tax cuts.

text.p: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell proposed a $2.52 billion spending budget for fiscal 1997-1998 that extends modest tax cuts and tries to ease the impact on the city's poor of federal and state welfare cuts.

The budget forecasts an adjusted operating deficit of $112 million, which would be covered by a surplus of the same amount carried over from the current year. The fund balance would be restored to $48 million in 1998-1999, according to city budget projections.

Rendell said in remarks for delivery to the City Council the budget was in many respects a "hold harmless" budget that would maintain city services, with the help of management and productivity savings.
But he also proposed increases to help compensate for federal and state social program cuts and to bolster recreation programs, the public library system and the police and fire departments.

The budget includes a 3.6 percent increase in revenues, to $2.46 billion, and a spending increase of 4.2 pct, to $2.51 billion. The operating surplus was projected at $50.5 million, before additonal adjustments for allocating the cost of new labor contracts and other items.
The budget proposes city-funded capital spending of $126.5 million in the fiscal year beginning July 1 1997, compared with $123.5 million the previous year.

Rendell proposed cutting the wage tax for city residents to 4.79 percent from 4.84 percent, reductions for non-residents also, and reducing a gross recepits tax on businesses to 2.875 mills from 2.95 mills.
This would be the third straight year of tax cuts. In addition, the city updated its five-year budget plan to include a seventh consecutive year of cuts, in the year 2002.
Tax cuts over the seven-year period would total 8.5 percent for wage taxes and nearly 13 percent for the overall business privilege tax, which includes the gross receipts provision.

However, Rendell said, the city faces difficult challenges coping with the cuts in federal and state welfare programs. He estimated the impact on the city's poor at $2.3 billion over the next five years.

The city's 1998-2002 five-year plan includes increases of $84 million compared with what was envisoned two years ago in its Department of Human Services, and increases of $10 million in programs for the homeless.

Rendell said visits to city health care centers have increased 14 percent in two years due to federal and state cuts, and the number of uninsured patients was expected to rise 21 percent in 1997-1998 compared with initial 1996-1997 estimates.
